item.title: [New York Post] Will Warren delivers in relief in final act of regular season as Yankees playoff role comes into view
item.dc:creator: Greg Joyce
item.description:
For a bullpen that has three (heavily used) sure things and a whole lot of question marks behind them entering the playoffs, Will Warren is trying to become one of the answers the Yankees will need to find. The right-handed starter made his final regular-season appearance out of the bullpen Friday and delivered 3 ¹/₃ scoreless innings in the Yankees’ 6-3 win over the Orioles to split the doubleheader, as he prepares for a relief role in the AL Wild Card Series and beyond.

item.content:encoded:
For a bullpen that has three (heavily used) sure things and a whole lot of question marks behind them entering the playoffs, Will Warren is trying to become one of the answers the Yankees will need to find.
The right-handed starter made his final regular-season appearance out of the bullpen Friday and delivered 3 ¹/₃ scoreless innings in the Yankees’ 6-3 win over the Orioles to split the doubleheader, as he prepares for a relief role in the AL Wild Card Series and beyond.

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Warren recorded seven of his 11 outs via the strikeout, racking up 13 whiffs on 28 swings and flashing the kind of swing-and-miss stuff that could be valuable in the Yankees bullpen.
“He can be big for us moving forward in the postseason, and in different roles,” manager Aaron Boone said.
The Yankees know they have workhorses Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn to form the bridge to David Bednar in the ninth inning, but they could certainly use more help. Warren has a chance to offer it, especially as his velocity and stuff has ticked up over the past month.
“I feel like as a starter, you’re supposed to get both sides of the plate out, so I think that would be pretty big for us,” said Warren, who finished the season with a 3.92 ERA. “You see Blackburn do it, you see Headrick do it, so whenever my name’s called, I’ll be ready to go.”
The club kept Warren to 54 pitches Friday in his third relief appearance of the season, ensuring he will be available on Tuesday for Game 1 against the Red Sox while also offering some length if needed.
“I felt good — a little less blackout this time,” Warren joked, referring to his bullpen cameo earlier this month against the Padres.
On a day when the wind from the incoming nor’easter wreaked some havoc, the Yankees (93-68) dropped the first game of the doubleheader 10-2 before taking the nightcap. Whether they actually play Game 162 on Sunday remains to be seen, with the forecast iffy, but their bats came alive in the second half of the twin bill, including a two-run double from Anthony Volpe and two hits apiece from Ben Rice and Ryan McMahon.
Former Met Pete Alonso crushed a pair of home runs for the Orioles (79-82) in Game 1 — including a 471-foot shot that cut through the wind blowing in — to move into sole possession of the American League lead with 43 on the year.
The Yankees also had some questionable outfield defense in both ends of the doubleheader, windy or not. In Game 1, Spencer Jones could not track down a fly ball to center field, as it hit off his glove and turned into an inside-the-park home run for Jeremiah Jackson. In Game 2, right fielder Heliot Ramos simply dropped a fly ball to right field.

item.content:encoded:
Ben Rice went 2-for-3 with a double, walk and a run scored as the Yankees topped the Orioles in the nightcap of Friday’s doubleheader.

Rice led off the home half of the first inning with a walk, but was cut down attempting to steal second base. item.content:encoded:
With the New York Yankees locked into an American League Wild Card berth, anticipation is building around who will make the final postseason roster—especially after former AL Rookie of the Year Luis Gil was optioned to the Florida Complex League ahead of October.
Gil was optioned alongside fellow right-hander Bradley Hanner, leaving one final roster spot up for grabs, as the Yankees announced on Thursday. While Gil had an opportunity to pitch his way onto the October roster, a rocky, walk-heavy outing against the Tampa Bay Rays sealed his fate.
In addition to bullpen decisions, the Yankees are closely monitoring their key injured stars as October approaches. On that front, manager Aaron Boone addressed the media to clear the air regarding conflicting reports about Aaron Judge’s status.
Boone also remains hopeful that slugger Giancarlo Stanton can return in time for the postseason, as the organization continues evaluating his physical readiness through live drills and simulated games.
Luis Gil #81 of the New York Yankees throws a pitch.
Yankees’ potential postseason roster
While the front office awaits definitive health updates on Judge, Stanton, and outfielder Trent Grisham, the baseline roster is coming into focus for their Wild Card showdown against the archrival Boston Red Sox, who are facing injury concerns of their own regarding catcher Willson Contreras.
Here is how the Yankees’ postseason roster is projecting:
- Starting Rotation: Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodón, Cam Schlittler, Will Warren
- Relief Pitchers: David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Michael Fulmer, Brent Headrick, Tim Hill, John Schreiber, Ryan Yarbrough
- Catchers: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
- Infielders: Jazz Chisholm Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Ryan McMahon, Anthony Volpe, José Caballero, Luis García Jr., Amed Rosario, George Lombard Jr., Ben Rice (1B/DH)
- Outfielders: Cody Bellinger, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones
As New York prepares for October baseball, fans are eager to watch the latest chapter in the game’s greatest rivalry unfold, with a spot in the ALDS against the division-champion Tampa Bay Rays hanging in the balance.
Key takeaways
- Luis Gil was optioned to the Florida Complex League ahead of October.
- Aaron Boone addressed conflicting media reports regarding Aaron Judge’s status.
- New York projects Gerrit Cole to lead its postseason starting rotation.

item.content:encoded:
On Friday, the New York Yankees will open up their final series of the 2026 regular season.
They have a doubleheader with the Baltimore Orioles in the Bronx.
Underdog MLB wrote (on Friday): “Orioles-Yankees will move Saturday’s game to a doubleheader on Friday due to weather.”
The Yankees are coming off a 6-4 win over the Tampa Bay Rays on Thursday (also in the Bronx).
Jazz Chisholm Jr. did not play.
Lineup For Game 1
For the first game on Friday, the Yankees have announced their starting lineup.
FantasyPros wrote: “NYY Yankees Lineup 09/25 Game 1 1. Paul Goldschmidt 1B 2. Ben Rice DH 3. Heliot Ramos LF 4. Amed Rosario RF 5. George Lombard SS 6. Spencer Jones CF 7. Anthony Volpe 3B 8. Ali Sanchez C 9. Jose Caballero 2B”
Chisholm Jr. remains out of the lineup on Friday.
The two-time MLB All-Star recently returned from the injured list.
He is batting .233 with 109 hits, 19 home runs, 55 RBIs, 69 runs and 41 stolen bases in 136 games this year.
It’s fair to assume that Chisholm Jr. will likely be back in the lineup on Friday night (for the second game).
Social Media Reacts To Jazz Being Out Of Lineup
Here’s what people were saying:
@Santo_Tripp: “Nastiest part of Volpe being at 3rd, surprisingly isn’t that they chose to do the experiment, it’s the fact that jazz isn’t even in the lineup. AND THAT’S THE WHOLE REASON HE IS BEING TRIED OUT AT THIRD!!!!”
@yanksjazz: “Is it possible Jazz will not play in round 1? Sox will throw 2 lefties”
@disyanks: “Sitting Jazz just long enough to make sure he’s cold against Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray? Boone is an idiot”
@rickcarter12: “Don’t need Jazz or McMahon since Red Sox will be starting lefties…Yanks can’t beat Gray or Tolle anyway..even when they had Judge and Stanton”
Looking At The Yankees
The Yankees are the second-place team in the American League East with a 92-67 record in 159 games.
They are 45-33 in 78 games at home.

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees were down four runs when Austin Wells came up in the sixth inning Thursday. His solo homer did not erase the deficit, but it got New York on the board. Two innings later, the Yankees had a 6-4 win over the Rays.
Wells finished 1-for-2 with a walk, two runs and a stolen base. It was his 14th home run of the season and his second since September 19. The Yankees have bigger bats, obviously. They still need something from the bottom of the order when a playoff starter handles the middle of it.
Wells is giving the Yankees more than one kind of at-bat
I liked the walk almost as much as the homer. Wells reached base twice and scored both times. The stolen base was another bit of pressure on Tampa Bay in a game that looked lost after five innings. New York got its decisive swing from George Lombard Jr., but Wells started the rally before the scoreboard made it interesting.
That matters because his job behind the plate is secure; his offensive production is the swing variable. A catcher hitting a homer once every few days changes the bottom third of a lineup. A catcher who can also take a walk gives the hitters behind him a chance to keep an inning alive.
October will test the bottom of the order
Two homers in six days do not guarantee a hot postseason. Wells has had cold stretches, and Thursday’s hit was his only one of the night. But he has picked up the bat at a useful time. With Ben Rice supplying middle-order power, the Yankees do not need Wells to carry the offense. They need him to make the opposing pitcher work and punish the occasional mistake. He did both Thursday.
More about:New York Yankees

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees did not just win on Wednesday night; they sent a loud message to the rest of the league. In a 9-2 blowout against the Tampa Bay Rays, the Bronx Bombers showed they are ready for the postseason grind. This was not a lucky break. It was a complete team performance that left the Rays staring at the scoreboard in disbelief.
Rice and McMahon Lead the Charge
Ben Rice stepped up in a massive way, hitting his 40th and 41st home runs of the season. He started the scoring by crushing the first pitch from Mason Englert into the right-field second deck. ESPN reports that Rice hit a solo home run in the fourth inning to finish his fifth career game with multiple homers. He finished with three hits and is now tied for the American League home run lead with stars like Pete Alonso and Yordan Alvarez. That is the kind of power the Yankees need right now.
Ryan McMahon also left his mark by hitting a grand slam while tying his career best with five runs batted in. In the third, he increased the lead to 7-0 with his third career slam. The Rays had no answer for this lineup. They allowed eight runs and nine hits in just 4 2/3 innings from Englert, who was brought up to give starters rest. The Yankees offense is firing on all cylinders as the playoffs approach.
Cole Keeps the Pitching Strong
Gerrit Cole was solid on the mound, allowing two runs and three hits over 5 2/3 innings. He threw a season-high 105 pitches and struck out eight batters despite the high pitch count. The 2023 AL Cy Young Award winner now holds a 3.61 ERA and 131 strikeouts across 22 starts since returning from Tommy John surgery. Per USA Today, he has been a steady force since coming back in May. The Yankees need him healthy and sharp for the division series, and this start proves he is ready.
While the Yankees offense soared, the Rays struggled to find their rhythm. George Lombard Jr. homered for New York, and Cedric Mullins went deep for Tampa Bay, but it was not enough. The Rays manager Kevin Cash admitted that left-hander Shane McClanahan will not recover in time for the Division Series. This injury news hurts Tampa Bay, but the Yankees have no time to celebrate their own health issues.
Playoff Stakes Get Real
New York is guaranteed to host a best-of-three AL Wild Card Series beginning Tuesday. The victor will meet the Rays in a best-of-five Division Series. The Yankees have the edge, but the playoffs are a different beast. They must stay focused.
This win was a statement of intent. The team is clicking at the right time. They have the power, the pitching, and the depth to go deep. The Rays clinched the AL East title a day before, but the Yankees proved they can beat them when it counts. The season is not over. The real work begins now.

item.content:encoded:
It's far too late to do anything about it this season, but the New York Yankees officially have a Ryan McMahon problem. It's been a year and a half now that he's been in pinstripes, and his performance with the bat has been worse than notorious frustrations like Joey Gallo, late-career DJ LeMahieu, and Isiah Kiner-Falefa, among others.
With a .208/.274/.344 line over 119 games this season, he has struggled against righties, is even more useless against lefties, and has arrived at a point where his good-but-not-great defense can no longer save his subpar bat.
Now that the case for an offseason DFA is clear, it's time to start thinking about potential 2027 replacements. There might not be a ton of high-end options, but there are a few that we can dream on.
Four dream Ryan McMahon replacements for 2027 if the Yankees shoot for the stars
Rafael Devers
Rafael Devers has been gaining buzz as a trade target for New York since the lead-up to the trade deadline. This would be a 180 in philosophy, as the whole reason things deteriorated between Devers and the Red Sox was growing concerns over his defense, and since arriving in San Francisco, he's primarily been a first baseman and DH. There's a school of thought, though, that George Lombard Jr.'s athleticism and defensive potential could help mitigate the defensive issues.
Devers hit 38 homers this year, and even a slow first half from him was light-years better than what McMahon has put up at any point in his career. Admittedly, this has become a bit more complicated due to questions about his status for Opening Day after undergoing core muscle surgery, and the Yankees would have to assume the vast majority of the nearly $200 million that the 29-year-old is owed, but his bat would be a perfect fit, and this would have the added benefit of tormenting Boston with a Raffy Revenge Tour.
Isaac Paredes
Another trade candidate, Isaac Paredes, could be an interesting option. The 27-year-old has long been on the Yankees' radar, and this winter could be their opportunity to get a deal done. The Houston Astros are never ones to help the Yankees out, but this could be a case where need aligns well enough for both squads that they have no other choice but to come to an agreement.
Houston is in a tough spot. Their horrid start put them behind the eight ball, and they're in a dogfight with the Texas Rangers for the AL West crown. The loser of the division chase might find themselves out of the Wild Card picture, and if that were to happen, it would mark the Astros' second consecutive playoff-less season. They've also fired general manager Dana Brown this summer, so changes are coming.
Paredes was subject to a slew of trade rumors last offseason because Houston has an infield logjam. Carlos Correa's injury cleared that up in 2026, but he'll be back next year and is under contract through at least 2028 (and possibly through 2032, depending on a series of vesting options). Meanwhile, they're also stuck with Christian Walker for another season, and Jose Altuve isn't going anywhere. Houston desperately needs pitching, and doesn't have a lot of room in their budget. Perhaps an Elmer Rodriguez-centric package could sway them.
Bo Bichette
It might sound strange, but Bo Bichette could be a sneaky-good solution for the Yankees. While he got off to a frigid start in Queens that has depressed his overall line, he's hit .291/.335/.440 since June 1. There's also some reason to believe that getting away from the Mets' dysfunction could help him rebound even more.
What's more, he could actually provide some things the Yankees need. Having another contact-forward bat would be nice, and he'd add some much-needed right-handed balance to the lineup. It seemed for a while that he was a shoo-in to opt in to his contract, but now, after a return to form, it's thought to be a 50-50 chance that he tests the free-agent market again this winter. If he does, he deserves a long look.
Zach Neto
This one requires some creativity, but there's a chance that New York could make this work. Zach Neto was the subject of a wave of trade rumors at the deadline, and according to Angels insider Jeff Fletcher of the OC Register, Los Angeles is expected to shop him again this offseason. The Red Sox and Rays were both rumored to be sniffing around the 25-year-old at the deadline, so making a deal for him could also be a defensive move.
Neto is a shortstop by trade, but if there's one knock on his game, it's that his range at the position is lacking. He does have a cannon for an arm, with his throwing power checking in at an 85th-percentile mark per Baseball Savant, so a move to the hot corner could maximize his defensive skill set.
The hiccup here will be the price. Neto is a perennial 30-30 candidate and doesn't hit free agency until 2030, so he won't be cheap to acquire. For this to work for the Yankees, they'd need to be able to hold onto Lombard Jr.; otherwise, they're simply trading one shortstop for another. That might not be possible on either team's end. Los Angeles acquired top prospect Arjun Nimmala from the Blue Jays for Jose Soriano, and the soon-to-be 21-year-old is tearing up Double-A. He could soon be ready to step in and take Neto's job.
This is the longest shot of them all, but it could help the Yankees extend their window well into Aaron Judge's decline. A core of Neto, Lombard Jr., Spencer Jones, Ben Rice, and Cam Schlittler could eventually usher in a new era without the club having to go through any sort of reset.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees erased a four-run deficit Thursday night, scoring six unanswered runs to rally past the Tampa Bay Rays, 6-4, in the series finale at Yankee Stadium.
Tampa Bay opened the scoring in the third inning after Taylor Walls walked and scored on a Yandy Díaz single that turned into an RBI double when Heliot Ramos’ throw toward third base got away. Junior Caminero followed with another run-scoring single.
Cam Schlittler made his final start of the regular season but was removed after three innings as the Yankees continued managing their starters’ workloads ahead of the postseason. Michael Fulmer and Tim Hill kept Tampa Bay in check before Caminero’s RBI double in the fifth extended the Rays’ lead to 3-0.
Tampa Bay added another run in the sixth after an error prevented the Yankees from completing a double play.
Austin Wells got New York on the board with a solo home run in the bottom half of the inning. The Yankees then erupted for three runs in the seventh.
George Lombard Jr. doubled home Ben Rice before scoring on a wild pitch. Paul Goldschmidt followed with a two-run single that tied the game at 4-4.
Lombard delivered again in the eighth, launching a two-run home run down the left-field line to put New York ahead. The homer was his seventh in 41 career games and gave him three runs batted in on the night.
Bradley Hanner protected the lead with a scoreless eighth and ninth innings to earn the first victory of his career.
Schlittler finished with a 1.95 earned-run average, a 0.92 walks-and-hits-per-inning ratio, 239 strikeouts and 47 walks across 193.2 innings in 33 starts.
The Yankees open their final regular-season series Friday against the Baltimore Orioles with a doubleheader beginning at 4:05 p.m. Game 2 will start no earlier than 7:05 p.m.

item.title: [amsterdamnews.com] Can the Yankees take down the Red Sox without Aaron Judge?
item.dc:creator: JAIME C HARRIS AmNews Sports Editor

item.content:encoded:
This was supposed to be the year the Yankees would win the franchise’s first World Series since 2009. A roster that included all-time greats Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera and Alex Rodriguez, Hall of Famer CC Sabathia, and Series MVP Hideki Matsui, one of the best players Japan has ever produced.
Yet, as the Yankees look towards Tuesday, when they open the playoffs at home against what is virtually certain to be the Boston Red Sox, their longtime nemesis, in a best-of-three wildcard series, the prospects of them navigating an always perilous path to the World Series were reduced when Yankees manager Aaron Boone said this past Tuesday that the reigning American League MVP likely won’t play in the series due to a right calf strain.
“We’re planning on him not being a part of that,” Boone revealed to reporters.
Judge, who has only appeared in 66 games this season, primarily recovering from a right rib stress fracture, which caused him to sit out 84 games from May 31 to Sept. 8, is now on the 10-day injured list, placed there last Friday. The 34-year-old Judge, arguably the best player in the sport over the last decade, isn’t expected back for the divisional round if the Yankees get by the Red Sox.
Last weekend, Boone informed the media the team didn’t have a firm estimate as to when Judge, a three-time AL MVP, three-time AL home run leader, two-time MLB RBI king and last season’s MLB batting champion, would return to the lineup.
“I mean, I have no idea, we’re in the early stages,” expressed Boone, now in his ninth season as the Yankees manager. “We’ll just obviously treat it and see what transpires.”
The Yankees watched Tampa Bay clinch the AL East title on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium when they won the second game of a double-header on Tuesday 6-1. The Yankees shut out the Rays in the opener. Tampa Bay 96-61 going into the third game of the four-game series last night with the finale scheduled for 7:05 tonight. The Yankees were second in the division at 90-67 and the 84-73 Red Sox third.
With Judge unavailable, the Yankees offense will have to be multifaceted — both power and small ball will be required to make a deep postseason run. Designated hitter Ben Rice, who as of Wednesday had 39 home runs and 95 RBIs, both team highs, was the only Yankee with more than 20 homers and 80 runs batted in, so timely power will have to come from sources such as second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. (19 home runs), first baseman Paul Goldschmidt (18), and left fielder Cody Bellinger (17).
But it is pitching that must advance the Yankees, led by leading AL Cy Young Award candidate Cam Schlittler, who is 14-6 with a 1.94 ERA and 234 strikeouts. Schlittler is scheduled to start tonight before taking the mound next week in the wildcard series.
But the prevailing question is: Can the Yankees win without Judge?

item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday night, the New York Yankees beat the Tampa Bay Rays (at home) by a score of 9-3.
They were led by Ben Rice, as he hit two home runs.
The Yankees wrote (via X): “Last night, Ben Rice became the third Yankee in franchise history to hit at least 40 HR within his first three Major League seasons, joining Aaron Judge and Joe DiMaggio 🙌”
Gerrit Cole Makes Rice Statement
Gerrit Cole got the start on Wednesday.
He allowed two earned runs (with eight strikeouts) in 5.2 innings.
After the game, Cole was asked about Rice (via YES Network).
Reporter: “We’ve seen a lot from Ben Rice over the last year-plus. But 40 and 41 now. What does it say about his continued development and what he really means to this lineup?”
Cole: “Super proud of him. Really exciting season for him. Deserves it too. He works really hard and puts in a lot of work behind the scenes. And had a great night tonight along with Mac. That was great to see along with George. Just keep plugging along. Those homers were huge for us. The offense played well. And we played pretty good defense in a tough environment tonight too. So overall really great, and a nice night for Ben.”
Looking At Rice
Rice was picked in the 12th round of the 2021 MLB Draft.
He is currently batting .263 with 148 hits, 41 home runs, 97 RBIs, 103 runs and three stolen bases in 151 games.
The 27-year-old has spent all three seasons of his MLB career with the Yankees.
Looking At Cole
Cole is in the middle of his 13th MLB season.
He has also had stops with the Pittsburgh Pirates and Houston Astros.
Right now, Cole is 10-9 with a 3.61 ERA in 22 starts.

item.content:encoded:
El número 41 apareció en la pantalla del Yankee Stadium y, por un instante, los Yankees volvieron a mirar hacia 1961.
Ben Rice conectó dos cuadrangulares el miércoles ante Tampa Bay para llegar a 41 en la temporada. El segundo puso al primera base de Nueva York en el mismo escalón de jonrones que Pete Alonso, Junior Caminero y Yordan Álvarez en la Liga Americana.
Pero el verdadero alcance de la noche va más allá de una carrera por el liderato de cuadrangulares. Rice acaba de entrar de lleno en la conversación por el MVP de la Liga Americana en la última semana del calendario. Sus números de temporada, después de 162 partidos para Nueva York, son 41 jonrones, 97 carreras anotadas, 148 hits, .263 de promedio, .362 de porcentaje de embasarse y .899 de OPS.
Al otro lado del clubhouse está Cam Schlittler.
El derecho de 25 años se convirtió en el brazo alrededor del cual gira la conversación por el Cy Young de la Americana. Después de 32 apariciones suma 14-6, 1.94 de ERA, 190.2 innings, 234 ponches y 0.91 de WHIP.
Pareja que entraría a los libros de historia de Yankees
Si Rice terminara conquistando el MVP y Schlittler el Cy Young, los Yankees volverían a tener en una misma temporada a los ganadores de los dos premios individuales más importantes de la Liga Americana. La última vez ocurrió en 1961.
Ninguno de los dos llegó a Nueva York con la etiqueta de fenómeno inevitable.
Rice fue elegido por los Yankees en la ronda 12 del Draft de 2021, con la selección 363, procedente de Dartmouth. Schlittler fue seleccionado en la séptima ronda de 2022, con el pick 220, después de jugar en Northeastern.
No fueron elecciones de primera ronda. No fueron nombres destinados desde el Draft a cargar con el uniforme de los Yankees.
Hoy, sin embargo, Rice es un bateador de 41 jonrones y Schlittler es el líder de una rotación que tiene al resto de la industria hablando del Cy Young. MLB describió recientemente la transformación de Schlittler como la de un séptima ronda convertido en All-Star y candidato al premio.
Y mientras Aaron Judge pasó buena parte de 2026 fuera por lesión, Rice terminó ocupando el espacio ofensivo que quedó abierto. Judge apenas disputó 66 encuentros y bateó .241 con 18 cuadrangulares.
¡Qué sucedió en 1961 para los Yankees!
Roger Maris y Whitey Ford escribieron una de las temporadas más reconocibles en la historia de la franquicia.
Maris bateó 61 cuadrangulares, rompió el récord de 60 que Babe Ruth había establecido en 1927 y terminó como MVP de la Liga Americana. En 161 partidos produjo .269/.372/.620, con 141 carreras impulsadas.
Ford, mientras tanto, tuvo una temporada que parecía diseñada para acompañar semejante hazaña: 25-4, 3.21 de ERA, 283 innings y 209 ponches. Ganó el Cy Young.
Los Yankees ganaron 109 juegos, conquistaron la Liga Americana por ocho juegos y después vencieron a Cincinnati en cinco partidos para ganar la Serie Mundial.
Existe además una precisión histórica importante. En 1961 todavía había un solo Cy Young para toda MLB. El premio comenzó a entregarse por separado en cada liga en 1967. Ford fue, por tanto, el ganador absoluto del Cy Young de 1961.
Rice no necesita batear 61 para entrar en esta conversación. Schlittler tampoco necesita reproducir exactamente los números de Ford.
Lo extraordinario sería que dos Yankees seleccionados fuera de las primeras rondas terminaran colocando sus nombres junto a Maris y Ford en la misma fotografía de premios.
¿Hay otros equipos con Cy Young y MVP en la misma temporada?
Antes de 1967, cuando el Cy Young era único para toda MLB, ocurrió con los Braves de 1957 —Hank Aaron y Warren Spahn—, White Sox de 1959 —Nellie Fox y Early Wynn—, Pirates de 1960 —Dick Groat y Vern Law— y Dodgers de 1962 —Maury Wills y Don Drysdale—.
Después de la división del premio por liga, la lista continuó con casos como Boston en 1986, Milwaukee en 1981, Oakland en 1990, Atlanta en 1991, Chicago White Sox en 1993, Oakland en 2002, St. Louis en 2005 y Minnesota en 2006. MLB registra 18 ocasiones en las que dos jugadores de un mismo equipo consiguieron MVP y Cy Young en la misma temporada hasta ese último caso.
También existe otra variante. Un mismo jugador ganó ambos premios en una temporada. Justin Verlander lo hizo en 2011, mientras Clayton Kershaw lo consiguió en 2014. En total, 11 pitchers han ganado Cy Young y MVP en el mismo año.
Por eso el último tramo de 2026 tiene una particularidad para Nueva York.
Today in 1961, Roger Maris of the @Yankees surpasses Babe Ruth’s record with his 61st homerun of the season. ⚾️
(📽 “61” released in 2001)#TodayInSports #PinstripePride
https://t.co/QJYClMw96G
Ben Rice y Cam Schlittler están en carrera por estos dos prestigiosos premios y también están intentando devolver a los Yankees a una fotografía que no aparece desde que Roger Maris y Whitey Ford hicieron historia hace 65 años.

item.title: [The Big Lead] Ben Rice joins list of Yankee legends featuring Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig & Joe DiMaggio
item.dc:creator: Matt Larter
item.description: The MLB season has seen Ben Rice etch his name alongside some of the greatest players in New York Yankees history. The 27-year-old slugger reached the 40-home run mark Wednesday during a 9-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays, putting him in an exclusive group of Yankees who have hit at least 40 home runs in a season at age 27 or younger. That list features legendary names including Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig and Mickey Mantle, all of whom accomplished the feat twice. Joe DiMaggio, Roger Maris, Aaron Ju
item.content:encoded:
The MLB season has seen Ben Rice etch his name alongside some of the greatest players in New York Yankees history.
The 27-year-old slugger reached the 40-home run mark Wednesday during a 9-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays, putting him in an exclusive group of Yankees who have hit at least 40 home runs in a season at age 27 or younger.
That list features legendary names including Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig and Mickey Mantle, all of whom accomplished the feat twice. Joe DiMaggio, Roger Maris, Aaron Judge and Juan Soto are also members of the group.
MORE: Blue Jays & Mariners make MLB history in worst way
Rice powers his way into Yankees history
Rice did not stop at one home run Wednesday, launching two against the Rays to reach 41 for the season. Through 151 games, he is batting .263 with 41 home runs and 97 RBI.
His power has been a major part of an impressive season, and reaching 40 home runs places Rice in company with some of the most celebrated sluggers to ever wear the Yankees uniform.
While Rice has already secured his place in the team’s statistical history, the Yankees are now preparing for the postseason.
Yankees prepare for the postseason
New York has clinched the American League’s top Wild Card position, holding a 10-game advantage over the Chicago White Sox, who occupy the final Wild Card spot. However, the Yankees will not be able to catch Tampa Bay for the AL East title.
The Yankees enter the final stretch of the regular season five games behind the Rays with only four games remaining. That leaves New York focused on preparing for the postseason rather than chasing the division crown.
The Yankees will send ace Cam Schlittler to the mound Thursday for the series finale against Tampa Bay. They will then close out the regular season with a three-game series against the Baltimore Orioles over the weekend.
For Rice, the final games offer an opportunity to build on a milestone season. At just 27 years old, his 40-home run campaign has already placed him alongside an extraordinary collection of Yankees legends, giving him a notable piece of franchise history heading into the postseason.

item.title: [New York Post] Yankees’ Austin Wells gets engaged to girlfriend in stunning beach scene: ‘Best off day’
item.dc:creator: Justin Terranova
item.description: It’s been an exciting September for Austin Wells off the field — and the Yankees hope there will be a thrilling October on it to match. The Yankees catcher got engaged to girlfriend Caroline Nielson earlier this month, according to photos she shared of the proposal on Instagram. The “forever and ever” caption suggests that the proposal took place Sept. 3 — an off day for the Yankees
item.content:encoded:
It’s been an exciting September for Austin Wells off the field — and the Yankees hope there will be a thrilling October on it to match.
The Yankees catcher got engaged to girlfriend Caroline Nielson earlier this month, according to photos she shared of the proposal on Instagram.
Nielson posted Wednesday photos of a touching beach scene with Wells down on one knee before the couple embraces.
The “forever and ever” caption suggests that the proposal took place Sept. 3 — an off day for the Yankees between series in California against the Angels and Padres.
They also included a photo of their daughter, Lucy, as part of the joyous moment.
Several significant others of Yankees teammates were quick to toast the couple in the comments section.
“My heart!!!!! Let’s get these two married!!! 🥹🥹🥹♥️♥️♥️♥️” wrote Ava O’Connor, who is dating outfielder Spencer Jones.
“The best off day in the history of off days,” wrote Carlos Rodon’s wife, Ashley.
“SCREAMING CRYING,” wrote Ben Rice’s girlfriend, Sara Falkson.
It is unclear when the couple first started dating. They announced that Nielson was expecting a child last November in one of the first public signs of a relationship.
Before the big day, Wells has an important postseason in front of him.
The 27-year-old catcher has somewhat rebounded from a miserable start to the season, pushing his average up to .185 after dipping down to .150 in July.
Wells, who is respected by the Yankees for his skills behind the plate, will likely be a mainstay in the lineup during the postseason.
Shop Yankees Merch
That will begin next week when the Yankees in all likelihood will take on the Red Sox in a best-of-three wild card series in The Bronx.
Wells did have perhaps his biggest moment in pinstripes when the rivals met last season in the same round, driving home the game-winning run with an eighth-inning single in Game 2.
The Yankees evened the series that night and went on to win Game 3 the following evening.
Now, Wells and the Yankees will look for an even deeper postseason run with Nielson no doubt cheering him on from the stands.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Ben Rice hopes to add to homer total as Yankees battle Rays

With four games remaining, Rice is among seven MLB players with at least 40 home runs, and he will attempt to continue his late-season surge Thursday night when New York hosts the Tampa Bay Rays, the American League East champion. item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge said he wants to return for next week’s wild-card series. Until he does come back, the slugger and the rest of the New York Yankees will be curious to see if slugger Ben Rice can homer again.
With four games remaining, Rice is among seven MLB players with at least 40 home runs, and he will attempt to continue his late-season surge Thursday night when New York hosts the Tampa Bay Rays, the American League East champion.
The Yankees (91-67) are assured of hosting the wild-card series and probably will face the Boston Red Sox for the second straight year. New York might be without Judge, who is dealing with a strained right calf after playing in seven games following being out with a fractured right rib.
On Monday, manager Aaron Boone described Judge’s strain as moderate and indicated he was not necessarily expecting the three-time American League MVP to be available. After the Yankees improved to 50-42 in games Judge has missed with Wednesday’s 9-2 rout of the Rays, the eight-time All-Star expressed confidence in his ability to return by next week.
“My goal is to come back as soon as I can,” Judge said. “If you ask me if I’m going to be back, I’m gonna tell you, yeah, I’m doing everything I can every single day I show up here to get back and be ready to go.”
Judge expressed confidence in his return after watching Rice hit a pair of solo homers on Wednesday, giving him 41 home runs in his second full season. Rice had three hits and a walk and is batting .349 with five homers in his past 12 games and .333 with seven homers and 17 RBIs in his past 27.
For the season, he is batting .263 with 97 RBIs after finishing with 26 homers, 65 RBIs and a .255 batting average last year.
“Each year, he’s gotten better,” Judge said of the 27-year-old. “Each month he’s gotten better. Even through bad slumps, he’s just making the reads and making the changes he needs to get back to his normal self. So it’s been fun to watch. He’s a complete player.”
Rice is hitting .381 against the Rays (96-62), who clinched the AL East with a 6-1 win over the Yankees on Tuesday night. After clinching, the Rays on Wednesday sat Yandy Diaz, who had a pair of two-run singles in the clincher.
Junior Caminero will be in the lineup to keep his streak of playing each game going but likely will be replaced after a few at-bats. Caminero took two at-bats and was lifted for a pinch hitter in the sixth.
“I just want to see good health and some guys freshened up,” Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash said. “It’s been a long season. They’ve played really hard to get to this point. Let’s find a way to continue to get our work in, and I know and trust that whoever’s on that field, they’re going to do everything they can to win games.”
Whoever is in the lineup for the Rays will face right-hander Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.94 ERA), who will make his final regular-season start before likely starting Game 1 of the wild-card series.
Since lasting 4 1/3 innings in an 8-2 loss to the Los Angeles Dodgers on July 19, Schlittler is 5-0 with a 1.46 ERA in his past 11 starts. The Yankees fell to 20-12 in his starts on Saturday when he allowed one earned run on three hits in six innings in a no-decision during a 5-3 loss at Arizona.
Schlittler is 1-2 with a 2.63 ERA in four career starts against the Rays.
Left-hander Ian Seymour (9-7, 4.38 ERA) originally was slated to start Wednesday but had his start pushed back a day to give Freddy Peralta extra rest to face Philadelphia on Friday.
Seymour is 0-1 with a 5.79 ERA in three starts this month, including Friday’s 4-2 loss to Boston when he allowed four runs on seven hits in five innings. One of his best starts this season occurred July 7 in Tampa Bay when he struck out 12 in 5 1/3 innings during a 6-4 win over the Yankees.
-Field Level Media

Rice told the reporters about the inspiration after he hit Nos. 40 and 41 in a 9-2 triumph over the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday in New York. He pointed at Boone after he hit the first pitch of the bottom of the first to right field for a 379-foot solo shot, emphasizing the manager-induced drive. "I think I said, 'hey, that's 40 for y
item.content:encoded:
Sept. 24 (UPI) -- New York Yankees designated hitter Ben Rice said he was inspired by manager Aaron Boone to reach the 40 home run milestone during the 2026 season.
Rice told the reporters about the inspiration after he hit Nos. 40 and 41 in a 9-2 triumph over the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday in New York. He pointed at Boone after he hit the first pitch of the bottom of the first to right field for a 379-foot solo shot, emphasizing the manager-induced drive.
"I think I said, 'hey, that's 40 for you, Skip,'" Rice said on the Prime Video broadcast. "I told him 'thank you so much for inspiring me to get to 40.'"
Boone predicted at spring training that Rice would reach 39 home runs in 2026. Rice told reporters Wednesday that he didn't really go into the campaign with a certain total in mind, but honed in on the 40 mark once he drew close over the final stretch of the season.
"It's a cool milestone," Rice said. "It's not something you go into the season really aiming for. You don't really know how it's going to go. But as I was approaching that number, it was definitely something I was hoping to achieve."
Yankees third baseman Ryan McMahon doubled the lead with an RBI single in the second inning. Shortstop George Lombardi Jr. raked a 384-foot solo homer in the third. McMahon, who went 2 for 4, hit a grand slam later in the inning for a 7-0 Yankees lead.
Rays right fielder Jonny DeLuca responded with an RBI double in the top of the fourth. Rice followed with a 383-foot solo shot to lead off the bottom of that frame.
Center fielder Cedric Mullins hit a 375-foot solo homer in the top of the fifth for the Rays' final run. Yankees right fielder Heliot Ramos plated the game's last score with a sacrifice fly in the eighth.
Rice went 3 for 4 with two RBIs, two runs scored and a walk. He hit .263, with 23 doubles, four triples and 97 RBIs, in addition to his American League-leading 41 homers, through 151 games this season.
"I was confident he was going to have a really big year," Boone said, when asked about Rice at his postgame news conference.
"I probably wanted to make sure it was just south of a [home run total] number, maybe to maybe let him know that."
Yankees starter Gerrit Cole allowed three hits and two runs over 5 and 2/3 innings to improve to 10-9 this season. Rays starter Mason Englert allowed nine hits and eight runs over 3 and 2/3 innings to drop to 0-4.
The Yankees (91-67) will host the Rays (96-62) in a series finale at 7:05 p.m. EDT Thursday in New York. They will start their final series of the season -- against the Baltimore Orioles -- on Friday at Yankee Stadium.

item.title: [Bozeman Daily Chronicle] Ben Rice tops Aaron Boone's preseason prediction of 39 homers, hitting 40th and then 41st

Boone predicted during spring training that Rice would finish with 39 home runs this season. Rice hit Nos. 40 and 41 in Wednesday night's 9-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays, tying for the American League home run lead. He smiled and pointed at Boone when he returned to the dugout after driving Mason Englert's first pitch of the game into Yankee Stadium's right field second deck. Rice grinned at B
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Ben Rice one-upped Aaron Boone. And then he two-upped the New York Yankees manager.
Boone predicted during spring training that Rice would finish with 39 home runs this season. Rice hit Nos. 40 and 41 in Wednesday night's 9-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays, tying for the American League home run lead.
He smiled and pointed at Boone when he returned to the dugout after driving Mason Englert's first pitch of the game into Yankee Stadium's right field second deck. Rice grinned at Boone some more after another solo homer in the fourth.
“I think I said, `Hey, there’s 40 for you,'” Rice recalled. “I was joking with him after the 41st one, saying, `Hey thanks for inspiring me this year.' But it’s all in good fun. Back in spring when he told me that, I knew that secretly meant he was hoping I’d hit 40.”
Rice is tied for the AL home run lead with Baltimore’s Pete Alonso, the Rays’ Junior Caminero and Houston’s Yordan Alvarez. He is hitting .263 and leads the Yankees with 97 RBIs and an .899 OPS, becoming a first-time All-Star and the biggest cog in an offense missing Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton for most of the season.
Boone deliberately picked an odd total rather than a round figure.
“I was confident he was going to have a really big year,” he said. “Probably wanted to make sure it was just south of a number, maybe to maybe let him know that.”
Rice, who had three hits and a walk, became the 13th Yankees player with a 40-home run season but just the third to reach the milestone during his first three seasons after Joe DiMaggio and Judge. Rice's plate appearances often prompt a rendition of Elton John's "Bennie and the Jets″ from the stadium's organist, and Rice has sparked an often struggling offense with 16 go-ahead homers this year and three that have tied games.
“One thing I always tell guys the difference between minor leaguers and big leaguers is the consistency,” Judge said. “He’s one of the best. I can look up at the clock and I know exactly where he’s going to be in the cage. You know what he’s doing in the training room, the weight room. It’s just every single day, man, this guy’s a machine.”
A 12th-round pick in the 2021 amateur draft from Dartmouth, where he played just 30 games over three years due to the coronavirus pandemic, Rice was mostly a catcher but occasionally a first baseman in the minors. He made his big league debut in June 2024 at age 25 after Anthony Rizzo broke a forearm.
Rice hit .171 with seven homers and 23 RBIs in 50 games that year, then batted .255 with 26 homers and 65 RBIs in 138 games last year.
With Stanton sidelined for most of the season, the left-handed-hitting Rice has 93 games at DH this year and 52 at first.
“It's tough to pull him off his back leg,” Yankees pitcher Gerrit Cole said. “He’s really able to stay balanced and deliver high-efficacy strikes on various pitches in all parts of the zone.”
Rice was hitting .306 through May, then batted .196 in June. An 18-for-58 (.119) slide after the All-Star break dropped his season average to .248 on Aug. 22 but he's rebounded to bat .333 (34 for 102) since.
“Went through a lull, which is inevitable, even in a great season,” Boone said. “Had a stretch in there where it was a struggle and he was grinding but kind of battled through that and feel like the last few weeks has been on a really good run.”
Rice's potential was evident on July 6, 2024, less than a month into his big league career, when he became the first Yankees rookie with three home runs in a game and tied Lou Gehrig's Yankees rookie record of seven RBIs. Consistency took time.
“A lot of it I always feel like is just experience-based,” Rice said. “You just see more pitching at the big league level, get exposed to guys who throw all different kinds of pitches from different angles and slots and all these things. I feel like I’ve always been a good learner in that way.”

item.title: [740thefan.com] MLB roundup: Padres climb to top of crowded NL wild-card standings
item.dc:creator: Thomson Reuters
item.description: By Field Level Media Sep 24 (Field Level Media) – Manny Machado homered and drove in three runs as the San Diego Padres moved to the brink of their third consecutive playoff appearance with a 5-1 road victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Wednesday. Fernando Tatis Jr. had three hits as the Padres reduced their magic number for clinching a National League wild-card spot to one. San Diego sits in the top NL wild-card position, one game ahead of both the Chicago Cubs and the Philadelphia Phillies
item.content:encoded:
By Field Level Media
Sep 24 (Field Level Media) – Manny Machado homered and drove in three runs as the San Diego Padres moved to the brink of their third consecutive playoff appearance with a 5-1 road victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Wednesday.
Fernando Tatis Jr. had three hits as the Padres reduced their magic number for clinching a National League wild-card spot to one. San Diego sits in the top NL wild-card position, one game ahead of both the Chicago Cubs and the Philadelphia Phillies.
San Diego won for the 14th time in its past 16 games while coming out on top for just the fourth time in 12 games against Los Angeles this season. The Padres have never reached the playoffs in three consecutive seasons.
In his return to the roster after recovering from knee and biceps injuries, Shohei Ohtani went 1-for-4 with a walk as the Dodgers saw their 11-game home winning streak end. Andy Pages and Teoscar Hernandez each had three hits while Los Angeles ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-9) gave up four runs (two earned) on five hits over six innings.
Brewers 4, Phillies 1
Brice Turang and Christian Yelich hit early home runs as visiting Milwaukee topped Philadelphia.
William Contreras knocked in two runs for the Brewers, who extended their franchise-record win total. Milwaukee needs to capture one of its final four games to reach 100 victories for the first time in team history. Logan Henderson (11-3) allowed one run in five innings.
Philadelphia starter Aaron Nola (7-11) permitted four runs and four hits in six innings. Bryson Stott doubled twice for the Phillies, who have a magic number of two to clinch a playoff berth.
Marlins 3, Cubs 2
Esteury Ruiz’s hustle enabled visiting Miami to score the go-ahead run in the seventh inning, leading to a win over Chicago.
After a video review, Ruiz was declared safe at second base on what was originally ruled an inning-ending double play, with Agustin Ramirez scoring to break a 2-2 tie. Cade Gibson (6-2) threw one perfect inning, and ace Sandy Alcantara recorded his second save.
Cubs starter Kevin Gausman allowed two runs in 5 2/3 innings, exiting after hurting his left shoulder while diving to make a tag at third base. Dansby Swanson hit a two-run single in the bottom of the sixth after Kyle Stowers socked a two-run homer in the top of the frame.
Diamondbacks 5, Rockies 3
Tim Tawa homered, Gabriel Moreno had three hits and Arizona continued its drive for a postseason berth with a win over Colorado in Denver.
The Diamondbacks have won four straight to move within three games of the Phillies and the Cubs in the chase for the last two NL wild-card positions with four games to play. Arizona starter Merrill Kelly (10-14) allowed two runs on four hits in 5 1/3 innings.
Ezequiel Tovar homered and finished with two hits for the Rockies, who lost for the 14th time in 16 games. Rookie Mason Adams (0-2) struck out a career- high eight over a career-best six innings. He yielded four runs, all unearned, on five hits.
Mariners 6, Astros 5 (10 innings)
Josh Naylor lined a one-out single to center field with the bases loaded in the bottom of the 10th inning to score the deciding run as Seattle kept its slim playoff hopes alive with a victory against visiting Houston.
Dominic Canzone drove in three runs for the Mariners, whose only chance to make the postseason is to finish in a three-way tie with Houston and Texas, who are tied atop the American League West. Julio Rodriguez’s bases-loaded walk tied the game before Naylor’s winning hit.
Yainer Diaz hit a tiebreaking triple in the top of the 10th inning after earlier belting a two-run homer for the Astros. Houston closer Josh Hader (4-2) took the loss.
Mets 7, Rangers 2
Marcus Semien damaged his former team’s playoff hopes when he hit a tiebreaking solo homer in the eighth inning to help New York prevail in Arlington, Texas.
Juan Soto socked a two-run homer in the third and Brett Baty added insurance with a pinch-hit grand slam in the ninth for the Mets. New York starter Nolan McLean (12-10) gave up two runs in seven innings.
The Rangers managed just four hits while losing their third game in a row. Jacob Latz (3-4) served up Semien’s homer.
Red Sox 1, Guardians 0
Andruw Monasterio’s sixth-inning RBI single and Sonny Gray’s six shutout innings propelled Boston past visiting Cleveland.
The Red Sox managed the lone run on 12 hits, all singles. They went 1-for-9 with runners in scoring position and left eight men on base through five innings before Monasterio’s run-scoring single broke the deadlock. Gray (18-5), who allowed four hits, increased his AL-leading win total.
Cleveland starter Foster Griffin (15-6) worked six frames, allowing one run on 10 hits. The Guardians remained tied with the White Sox atop the AL Central.
Royals 5, White Sox 4
Maikel Garcia’s tiebreaking double in the seventh inning capped a three-hit, three-RBI night as Kansas City beat visiting Chicago.
While the Royals snapped a five-game skid, the White Sox missed a chance to regain control of the AL Central and clinch a playoff berth.
Connor Thomas (2-1) tossed two shutout innings for the win, and Steven Cruz recorded his eighth save. Kansas City’s Carter Jensen and Chicago’s Braden Montgomery each had three hits and a run.
Braves 3, Reds 2 (10 innings)
Mauricio Dubon’s infield chopper to the mound in the 10th inning gave host Atlanta a walk-off victory over Cincinnati.
Braves starter Chris Sale pitched 5 2/3 innings and allowed one run while striking out 10, reaching 200 strikeouts for the ninth time in his career. Matt Olson and Austin Riley homered for Atlanta, and Brent Suter (3-2) tossed a perfect top of the 10th.
Juan Brito led off the game with a home run, and he and Matt McLain each had two hits for the Reds. Cincinnati starter Andrew Abbott fired a season-high seven innings and allowed two runs.
Orioles 4, Blue Jays 2 (Game 1)
Baltimore’s Pete Alonso hit another home run and the Orioles eliminated visiting Toronto from playoff contention by winning in the first game of a doubleheader.
The Blue Jays were the reigning American League champions, but they won’t have a chance to return to the World Series.
Chris Bassitt (9-5) pitched five-plus innings to notch a victory in his third consecutive start. He gave up two runs on seven hits. Max Scherzer (3-9) surrendered four runs and four hits in five innings.
Orioles 4, Blue Jays 2 (Game 2)
Christian Encarnacion-Strand homered and drove in three runs and Trey Gibson took a shutout into the seventh inning as Baltimore completed a doubleheader sweep of visiting Toronto to stay in playoff contention.
Baltimore must win its remaining three games and have the White Sox lose their remaining four in order to have a chance for an AL wild-card spot. Gibson (2-3), a rookie who hadn’t pitched in the major leagues since June 30, gave up three hits in 6 2/3 innings.
Davis Schneider hit a two-run ninth-inning homer off Felix Bautista in the nightcap for the Blue Jays. Toronto rookie starter CJ Van Eyk (0-2) allowed four runs on four hits in five innings.
Yankees 9, Rays 2
Ryan McMahon hit a third-inning grand slam and tied a career high with five RBIs while Ben Rice hit a pair of solo homers as host New York rolled past Tampa Bay.
McMahon drove in five runs for the fourth time in his career. Rice homered on the first pitch of the contest to become the 13th Yankee with 40 homers in a season. He later hit his 41st. Gerrit Cole (10-9) allowed two runs on three hits in 5 2/3 innings.
Jonny DeLuca hit an RBI double and Cedric Mullins homered for the Rays. Mason Englert (0-4) allowed eight runs on nine hits over 3 2/3 innings.
Nationals 4, Tigers 2
Yohandy Morales hit a two-run homer and visiting Washington held on for a victory over Detroit as the Nationals won the three-game series 2-1.
Brady House had two hits and scored a run while CJ Abrams, who homered twice on Tuesday, reached base three times and knocked in a run for Washington. Will Dion (2-2) tossed two innings of one-run relief, and Yovanny Cruz got four outs for his first career save.
Detroit starter Framber Valdez (10-12) gave up two runs and four hits over 5 1/3 innings. Ben Malgeri homered and drove in both of the Tigers’ runs, and Kevin McGonigle added three hits.
Twins 4, Giants 2
Pinch hitter Walker Jenkins broke a seventh-inning tie with an RBI single as Minnesota completed a 4-3 road trip with a win over San Francisco.
Luke Keaschall drove in two runs with a homer and a sacrifice fly while Josh Bell added an RBI single for the Twins. Yoendrys Gomez (3-4) threw 1 2/3 innings of scoreless relief, and Andrew Morris escaped a ninth-inning jam for his fifth save.
Shay Whitcomb had two hits for the Giants, who have lost five out of six. Reliever Dylan Smith (0-6) yielded two runs while getting just two outs.
Cardinals 5, Pirates 1
Matthew Liberatore struck out six over 5 2/3 innings and JJ Wetherholt had three hits and an RBI to lead St. Louis to a victory at Pittsburgh.
Liberatore (6-14) allowed only one run — on a solo homer by Brandon Lowe — as the Cardinals snapped the Pirates’ season-high-tying five-game winning streak. St. Louis’ Jose Fermin went 2-for-4.
Lowe had two hits and Ryan O’Hearn added two doubles for Pittsburgh. Pirates reliever Brandon Eisert (3-3) gave up three runs in two-thirds of an inning.
Athletics 7, Angels 3
Rookie Henry Bolte recorded the first four-hit game of his career and Donovan Walton hit a three-run homer to help the Athletics top Los Angeles in West Sacramento, Calif.
Shea Langeliers had a two-run double and Bolte scored twice, had two doubles and drove in one run for the A’s, who assured they will avoid a 100-loss season. Geoff Hartlieb (2-1) threw 1 2/3 innings of scoreless relief.
Mike Trout and Vaughn Grissom homered for the Angels, who are two losses shy of the first 100-loss season in franchise history. Walbert Urena (9-11) allowed five runs and seven hits over four innings.
(–Field Level Media)

item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.description: PHILADELPHIA -- Christian Yelich and Brice Turang hit solo home runs, and the Milwaukee Brewers delayed Philadelphia's potential postseason clinch with a 4-1 win over the Phillies on Wednesday night. item.content:encoded:
PHILADELPHIA -- Christian Yelich and Brice Turang hit solo home runs, and the Milwaukee Brewers delayed Philadelphia's potential postseason clinch with a 4-1 win over the Phillies on Wednesday night.
The Phillies needed both a win over the Brewers and a loss later Wednesday night by either Arizona or San Diego to secure their fifth straight trip to the National League playoffs. The Phillies started their run with a trip to the World Series in 2022, reached the NL Championship Series the next season and are coming off consecutive NL East titles.
The Phillies have to settle for a wild-card berth this season and are likely to open the playoffs next week on the road. The Phillies, Chicago and San Diego hold the three NL wild cards headed into the final games of the season.
The Phillies went 0 for 12 with runners in scoring position against the Brewers and left 10 runners on base.
Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said ahead of the game the team was willing to wait at Citizens Bank Park until after the Padres game ended, if necessary, to celebrate. No need to hang around.
Aaron Nola (7-11) had turned around a miserable season and posted a 1.86 ERA over his past eight starts as the longest-tenured Phillie got the chance to clinch. With a playoff party looming, he instead surrendered Turang's 20th homer of the season in the first inning and Yelich's 12th of the year in the second.
The Phillies scored their only run in the second inning after loading the bases with no outs against Brewers starter Logan Henderson (11-3). Henderson allowed four hits and one run over five innings to help the NL Central champion Brewers win their 99th game of the season.
MARLINS 3, CUBS 2 Kyle Stowers homered and Miami denied host Chicago a chance to clinch a playoff berth for the second straight night with a victory. Dansby Swanson drove in both runs for the Cubs, who needed a win or an Arizona loss to Colorado to secure an NL wild-card berth. Joe Mack's groundout brought home Augustin Ramirez with the go-ahead run in the seventh and the Marlins retired the next nine Chicago batters to win their second straight game after dropping three in San Diego.
DIAMONDBACKS 5, ROCKIES 3 Corbin Carroll had a two-run triple to cap a four-run first inning and visiting Arizona kept its playoff hopes alive with a victory over Colorado. Gabriel Moreno drove in the first run and finished with three hits to help Arizona (84-74) close within three games of the Phillies and Cubs for an NL wild card.
CARDINALS 5, PIRATES 1 Matthew Liberatore ended an 11-start winless stretch and Alec Burleson got his major league-best 112th RBI as St. Louis defeated host Pittsburgh. Liberatore (6-14) gave up 1 run and 6 hits in 5 2/3 innings with 6 strikeouts and no walks.
BRAVES 3, REDS 2 (10) Chris Sale struck out 10 and reached 200 strikeouts for the season, Mauricio Dubon delivered a winning RBI single in the 10th inning, and host Atlanta defeated Cincinnati.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
ORIOLES 4-4, BLUE JAYS 2-2 Pitcher Trey Gibson was strong into the seventh inning and host Baltimore beat Toronto to sweep a doubleheader and at least temporarily stay alive in the American League playoff race. One more loss by the Orioles -- or a win by the Chicago White Sox, who lost at Kansas City on Wednesday night -- would eliminate Baltimore. The Orioles also won the opener 4-2. The 24-year-old Gibson (2-3) allowed 3 hits in 6 2/3 scoreless innings with 7 strikeouts and 2 walks in his eighth career start
ROYALS 5, WHITE SOX 4 Maikel Garcia had three hits and three RBI, including a tiebreaking, run-scoring double in the seventh inning, as host Kansas City beat the White Sox and delayed Chicago's bid for a postseason berth.
RED SOX 1, GUARDIANS 0 Sonny Gray pitched six innings to tie Philadelphia's Cristopher Sanchez for the major league lead with his 18th victory, Andruw Monasterio drove in the only run with a sixth-inning single and host Boston edged Cleveland to snap the Guardians' six-game winning streak. Gray (18-5) allowed 4 singles, struck out 3, walked 1 and lowered his ERA to 2.72.
YANKEES 9, RAYS 2 Ben Rice hit his 40th and 41st home runs, Ryan McMahon added a grand slam while matching his career high with five RBI and host New York beat Tampa Bay. Gerrit Cole (10-9) allowed 2 runs and 3 hits in 5 2/3 innings with 8 strikeouts and 3 walks for the Yanks.
INTERLEAGUE
NATIONALS 4, TIGERS 2 Yohandy Morales homered for the second time in three games and Washington beat host Detroit. Washington has won eight of its past 11 games. Detroit has lost six of eight.
TWINS 4, GIANTS 2 Pinch-hitter Walker Jenkins hit an RBI single in the seventh inning allowed visiting Minnesota to win its second straight over San Francisco.
METS 7, RANGERS 2 Marcus Semien hit a tiebreaking homer in the eighth inning against his former team and Brett Baty added a pinch-hit grand slam in the ninth as New York beat host Texas. Rookie right-hander Nolan McLean (12-10) allowed 2 runs and 3 hits over 7 innings for the last-place Mets, who have won both games in Texas since ex-interim manager Andy Green was given the full-time position Tuesday.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

24 Sep 2026, 07:55 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Brad Penner)
Ryan McMahon hit a third-inning grand slam and tied a career high with five RBIs, while Ben Rice hit a pair of solo homers as the host New York Yankees rolled to a 9-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night.
McMahon drove in five runs for the fourth time in his career and started his big night with a two-strike single off Tampa Bay spot starter Mason Englert (0-4) for a 2-0 lead in the second.
After George Lombard Jr. started the third with a homer to right-center field, McMahon lifted a full-count offering down the right field line for a 7-0 lead.
It was the third baseman's third career grand slam, and McMahon went deep after Anthony Volpe took ground balls at third before the game.
Rice homered on the first pitch of the contest from Englert to become the 13th Yankee with 40 homers in a season. After hitting his fourth career leadoff homer, Rice homered again into the right field seats for an 8-1 lead in the fourth.
Rice had his fifth career multi-homer game and became the seventh player to reach 40 homers this season. Rice also added a single and reached base four times.
The Yankees (91-67) won for the 10th time in 15 games. Rookie Spencer Jones doubled and scored on McMahon's RBI single in the second, while Heliot Ramos chipped in a sacrifice fly.
New York's Gerrit Cole (10-9) allowed two runs on three hits in 5 2/3 innings in a postseason tuneup. Cole struck out eight, walked three and reached double-digit victories for the 10th time in his career.
Jonny DeLuca hit an RBI double, and Cedric Mullins homered for the Rays (96-62), who fell three games behind Milwaukee for the best record in baseball.
After clinching their fifth AL East title on Tuesday, the Rays rested AL hits leader Yandy Diaz and played Junior Caminero for five innings.
Englert allowed eight runs on nine hits over 3 2/3 innings after Ian Seymour was originally slated to start for Tampa Bay. Seymour is expected to pitch in Thursday's series finale.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [Bronx Pinstripes] Schlittler Makes Franchise History, Yankees Bury Angels With Five-Run…
item.dc:creator: Jimmy Spiro

Cam Schlittler made sure it didn't get out of hand. Austin Wells made sure it never got to an 11th. item.content:encoded:
Yankees 6, Angels 3, and for eight and a half innings Wednesday night at Angel Stadium, this one looked like it might stay 1-1 into the parking lot. Cam Schlittler made sure it didn't get out of hand. Austin Wells made sure it never got to an 11th.
Wells' two-out, bases-loaded single in the 10th was the whole game in one swing -- a 1-2 fastball from Luke Murphy that found right field, scoring two and flipping a tossup into a laugher. By the time the inning was over, the Yankees had scored five runs on four straight singles and taken the rubber match of the series, 2-1.
The Turning Point
Extra innings started with Amed Rosario parked on second, the automatic runner, and it took a while to cash him in. José Caballero singled to send him to third. Jazz Chisholm Jr. walked to load the bases. Luis García Jr. popped out for the second out, and for a second it looked like the Yankees might strand the whole mess (they'd left 14 men on base by night's end, which tells you something about how stubborn this offense had been all night).
Then Wells got to Murphy. Two runs scored, Chisholm to third. Cody Bellinger singled him home. Trent Grisham singled Wells home. Ben Rice singled in Bellinger. Four hitters, four singles, five runs, and the Angels never got the third out they needed to escape it.
Star of the Game: Schlittler Rewrites the Record Book
Before any of that happened, Schlittler spent eight innings quietly making history. Two hits. One run. Nine strikeouts. Zero walks. Ninety-nine pitches, 71 of them strikes -- the kind of start where you check the line twice because it doesn't look real for a guy facing a lineup with Mike Trout in it.
That was the 19th time this season Schlittler has allowed a run or fewer in a start. That's a new Yankees single-season record, passing the mark of 18 shared by Ron Guidry's 1978 Cy Young season, Whitey Ford in 1964, and Jack Chesbro all the way back in 1904. Good company. Better yet, Schlittler's still adding to it.
He didn't get the win (no decision, if you're scoring at home), because the Yankees' bats needed extra innings to back him up. He also didn't seem to care. That's usually the sign of the right kind of pitcher.
Detmers Made Him Earn It
Give the Angels' Reid Detmers his due, too. Seven innings, six hits, one earned run, eight strikeouts of his own -- the only damage against him a ground-rule double by Rosario in the fourth that scored Bellinger. For seven innings, this was a legitimate pitchers' duel between two guys who deserved a better final line than "no decision."
Vaughn Grissom's solo homer off Schlittler in the seventh tied it at 1-1 and set up the standoff that lasted until the 10th blew it open.
Boone's Bullpen Math Worked, Barely
David Bednar came in for a scoreless ninth -- one hit, three strikeouts -- and got the win when the Yankees broke through an inning later, which is how it works even if Bednar didn't throw a single pitch in the inning that decided it. Michael Fulmer took the 10th with a five-run lead and made it interesting, giving up a two-run homer to Moisés Ballesteros that scored the Angels' own automatic runner, Wade Meckler. Fulmer got the next two outs anyway. A laugher stayed a win, which is really all that matters in the box score.
Yankees take the series 2-1 after dropping the opener 1-10 on Monday, and they move to 80-60, three and a half back of the Rays with a month to play. San Diego's up next.
Jimmy writes the Bronx Pinstripes game recap after every Yankees game. Beat-reporter pacing, fan's heartbeat. He calls opposing players by last name and has no patience for dead-air innings.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees (91-67) defeated the Tampa Bay Rays (96-62) 9-2 on Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium to take a 2-1 lead in the four-game series.
The win comes a day after the Rays clinched the American League East championship. Ben Rice hit his 40th home run for the Yankees in the first inning, and his 41st homer in the fourth. After New York added a single run in the second, they broke through with five in the third, thanks in part to a grand slam from Ryan McMahon.
The Rays offense came from Jonny DeLuca, who hit a RBI double in the fourth, and Cedric Mullins who hit a solo homer in the fifth. Mason Englert (0-4, 5.95) took the loss for the Rays, allowing eight earned runs on nine hits in three and two-third innings in which he struck out six and walked one.
The Rays will now try to split the four-game series when they meet in the finale on Thursday night. Ian Seymour (9-7, 4.38) is scheduled to start for the Rays and face Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.94) for New York. First pitch Thursday is scheduled for 7:05 PM - pregame coverage begins with Ronnie Lane hosting Inside Pitch at 6:00 PM on 95.7 WDAE & AM 620, your Home of Rays Baseball.
COVER PHOTO COURTESY GETTY IMAGES

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK –- Durante el reciente viaje de los Yankees a Phoenix, Aaron Boone se reclinó detrás del escritorio de una oficina, claramente satisfecho con su capacidad para hacer pronósticos. Meses atrás, había predicho que Ben Rice terminaría con 39 jonrones, una cifra que le pareció baja a uno de los interesados.
“Ya sabes lo que está tratando de hacer”, dijo Rice entonces. “Estaba tratando de provocarme un poco. Le gusta quedarse una o dos por debajo de lo que quizás sería tu meta”.
Rice debería apreciar más esta cifra: Su actuación de dos cuadrangulares la noche del miércoles le permitió compartir el liderato de jonrones de la Liga Americana. Ryan McMahon conectó un grand slam y George Lombard Jr. también se voló la cerca, impulsando a los Yankees a una victoria por 9-2 sobre los Rays en el Yankee Stadium.
Con 41 vuelacercas, la mayor cantidad del equipo, Rice igualó a Pete Alonso, de los Orioles, Yordan Álvarez, de los Astros, y Junior Caminero, de Tampa Bay, con la mayor cantidad en la Liga Americana. La cifra representa un récord personal para Rice, quien recibió su primer llamado al Juego de Estrellas este verano y se perfila como una pieza integral de la producción ofensiva de los Yankees en los playoffs.
Rice se unió a Aaron Judge (cuatro veces) como los únicos jugadores seleccionados por los Yankees en el Draft que han conectado al menos 40 bambinazos en una temporada. Judge (2017), Rice (2026) y Joe DiMaggio (1937) son los únicos jugadores de los Yankees que han tenido una campaña de 40 jonrones dentro de sus primeros tres años de carrera.
McMahon remolcó cinco carreras y los Yankees ganaron por décima ocasión en 14 juegos.
Gerrit Cole limitó a Tampa Bay a dos anotaciones y tres hits en 5.2 innings, realizando 105 pitcheos, 63 de ellos strikes, su mayor cantidad de la temporada, en su última apertura de la campaña regular. El derecho se prepara para una esperada asignación en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Cole otorgó tres bases por bolas y ponchó a ocho, permitiendo un cuadrangular de Cedric Mullins en la quinta entrada. Cole terminó el año con récord de 10-9 y efectividad de 3.61 en 22 aperturas, luego de regresar a finales de mayo de una cirugía Tommy John a la que se sometió en marzo del 2025.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Ben Rice hit his 40th and 41st home runs, Ryan McMahon added a grand slam while matching his career high with five RBIs and the New York Yankees beat the Tampa Bay Rays 9-2 on Wednesday night.
Gerrit Cole (10-9) allowed two runs and three hits in 5 2/3 innings and a season-high 105 pitches with eight strikeouts and three walks. The 2023 AL Cy Young Award winner had a 3.61 ERA and 131 strikeouts over 22 starts and 127 innings following his return in May from Tommy John surgery.
A day after Tampa Bay clinched the AL East title, Rice hit the first pitch of the first inning from Mason Englert (0-4) into the right-field second deck for his fourth career leadoff homer and second this season.
Rice added a solo drive in the fourth for his fifth career multihomer game and finished with three hits. He is tied for the AL home run lead with Baltimore's Pete Alonso, the Rays' Junior Caminero and Houston's Yordan Alvarez.
George Lombard Jr. also homered for the Yankees and Cedric Mullins went deep for the Rays.
New York is assured of hosting a best-of-three AL Wild Card Series starting Tuesday, likely against Boston. The winner will face the Rays in a best-of-five Division Series.
McMahon had an RBI single in the second and boosted the lead to 7-0 in the third with his third career slam.
Englert, brought up to allow Rays starters extra rest ahead of the playoffs, allowed eight runs and nine hits in 4 2/3 innings.
Rays manager Kevin Cash said left-hander Shane McClanahan won't recover in time for the Division Series but left-hander Garrett Cleavinger and right-hander Tyler Wells are possibilities. All three have forearm tightness.
Up next
Yankees RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.94 ERA) and Rays RHP Freddy Peralta (9-11, 4.56) start Thursday night's series finale.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – During the Yankees’ recent trip to Phoenix, Aaron Boone leaned back behind an office desk, clearly pleased by his prognostication ability. Months ago, he’d forecast that Ben Rice would finish with 39 home runs, a tally that seemed light to one interested party.
“You know what he’s trying to do,” Rice said then. “He was trying to get under my skin a little bit there. He likes to just short you one or two of maybe what your goal would be.”
Rice should appreciate this number more: His two-homer performance on Wednesday evening earned a share of the American League home run lead. Ryan McMahon hit a grand slam and George Lombard Jr. also went deep, powering a 9-2 victory over the Rays at Yankee Stadium.
With a team-leading 41 home runs, Rice tied the Orioles' Pete Alonso, Yordan Alvarez of the Astros and Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero for the most in the AL. The mark is a career high for Rice, who earned his first All-Star selection this past summer and projects to be an integral part of the Yanks’ playoff production.
Rice joined Aaron Judge (four times) as the only Yankees Draft picks to hit at least 40 home runs in a season. Judge (2017), Rice (‘26) and Joe DiMaggio (1937) are the only Yanks to have a 40-homer season within the first three years of his career.
McMahon drove in five runs as the Yankees won for the 10th time in 14 games.
Gerrit Cole limited Tampa Bay to two runs and three hits over 5 2/3 innings, throwing a season-high 105 pitches (63 strikes) in his final start of the regular season. The right-hander is preparing for an expected assignment in the AL Wild Card Series.
Cole walked three and struck out eight, surrendering a fifth-inning homer to Cedric Mullins. Cole finished the year with a 10-9 record and 3.61 ERA in 22 starts, having returned in late May from Tommy John surgery performed in March 2025.

item.content:encoded:
Ben Rice is in the process of wrapping up a breakout season for the New York Yankees. That included making some history on Wednesday.
Facing the Tampa Bay Rays, the All-Star first baseman opened the scoring in the first inning with his 40th homer of the season. It was a second-deck no-doubter off a first-pitche sinker from Rays starter Mason Englert.
Then he hit another in the fourth inning, putting him in a four-way tie for the AL lead at 41 homers with Pete Alonso, Yordan Álvarez and Junior Caminero.
By reaching 40 homers in a season, Rice has entered rare territory. As MLB.com's Sarah Langs notes, he joins teammate Aaron Judge as the second Yankees draft pick to post a 40-homer season.
Yes, only the second.
Obviously, the Yankees have more than fair share of elite sluggers in history. It's just that many of the homegrown ones entered the league before 1965, when the MLB Draft was first instituted. Others began their careers with other teams before joining the Yankees.
Here is the complete list of Yankees players to post a 40-homer season and how they joined New York, with pre-draft players italicized:
- Aaron Judge (draft pick)
- Roger Maris (trade)
- Mickey Mantle (signed)
- Lou Gehrig (signed)
- Joe DiMaggio (signed)
- Tino Martinez (trade)
- Reggie Jackson (free agent)
- Ben Rice (draft pick)
There are other Yankees draft picks who have come close, with Fred McGriff, Steve Balboni and Don Mattingly all posting a season with at least 35 homers.
McGriff, a ninth-round Yankees pick in 1981, came closest to 40 among that group with 37 in a 1993 season split between the Atlanta Braves and San Diego Padres. He never played a game for New York, having been traded as minor leaguer in a now-infamous deal for Dale Murray and Tom Dodd.
As for some other famous names, Derek Jeter never hit more than 24 and Bernie Williams never hit more than 30.
It's all a fun little quirk of history, created by the flow of both the Yankees and the MLB rulebook through the time. It actually requires quite a lot to go right for a draft pick to hit 40 homers in even a single season.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Aaron Judge's latest injury offers a glimpse of a rapidly approaching Yankees future
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz
